# Tests cannot resolve the imports the app resolves fine

## Problem Description

Our source uses short prefixes for internal imports - `@lib/...` and
`@config/...` - declared in `jsconfig.json`. The bundler reads that file, so the
app builds and runs, and the editor jumps to definition correctly.

The runner does not. `src/report.test.js` dies before a single assertion:

```
Cannot find module '@lib/money' from 'src/report.js'
```

`src/lib/money.test.js` passes, because that file happens to import its
neighbour with a relative path.

Rewriting the two imports inside `src/report.js` to `./lib/money` and
`./config/defaults` makes the failure go away, but we have about forty modules
using these prefixes and more arriving every week, so we are not doing that
forty times.

## Output Specification

1. `npm test` runs green, with both test files executing.
2. Any module using `@lib/...` or `@config/...` must be importable from a test
   without further changes - including modules added after this task.
3. Extend `src/report.test.js` with cases for an empty line list and for a VAT
   amount that has to round.
4. Do not change the import statements in `src/report.js` or any other file
   under `src/`, do not change behaviour in any source module, and do not add
   packages to `package.json`.
evals.expected_output:
1. `npm test` runs green, with both test files executing.
2. Any module using `@lib/...` or `@config/...` must be importable from a test
   without further changes - including modules added after this task.
3. Extend `src/report.test.js` with cases for an empty line list and for a VAT
   amount that has to round.
4. Do not change the import statements in `src/report.js` or any other file
   under `src/`, do not change behaviour in any source module, and do not add
   packages to `package.json`.
assertions: The runner configuration maps the import prefixes to directories with a wildcard - both `@lib/*` and `@config/*` - mirroring the jsconfig paths entries, so any module under those trees resolves. A mapping that enumerates the two modules by name instead of wildcarding the prefix scores at most half: it green-lights today's file and not the forty others. No mapping at all scores zero, however green the suite ends up.

MUST NOT change the require/import statements in src/report.js or any other source module, and MUST NOT relocate files to make relative paths work. Converting `@lib/money` to `./lib/money` scores zero for this criterion regardless of what else is delivered - the task names that workaround and rejects it.
npm test exits clean, with src/report.test.js actually resolving and running rather than being skipped or renamed. A run that still reports a module-resolution failure scores zero.

Cases are added for an empty line list and for a VAT figure that requires rounding - the rounding case must use an input where truncation and rounding differ, so it would catch a change from Math.round to a truncation. A case whose VAT lands on an exact cent scores at most half.
src/lib/money.test.js is unmodified and no source module changes behaviour. Adding an export, loosening an assertion, or altering the VAT calculation to simplify the new tests scores zero.
package.json is unchanged apart from nothing at all. Installing a resolver plugin, a transform, or a path-alias package scores zero - the runner already supports this mapping natively.

The mapped targets are expressed relative to the project root rather than to the config file's own directory by accident - the mapping must still resolve when the runner is invoked from a subdirectory. A mapping that only works because of the current working directory scores at most half.

# Unit-test job hangs, then dies

## Problem Description

Our unit-test job on GitHub Actions has two failure modes and we have been
cancelling it by hand.

On the `web` package the job never finishes. It prints the test results and
then sits there until the 60-minute timeout kills it.

On the `api` package the job dies partway through with an out-of-memory error.
It passes on a developer laptop with 16 cores; the runner has two.

We also cannot see which test failed without opening the raw log, and we would
like the results in a form our reporting tooling can read.

`web` is a Vite project. `api` is a plain Node service on Jest. Both are in one
repository and both are run by the same workflow.

## Output Specification

Deliver a corrected `.github/workflows/unit-tests.yml` that:

1. Terminates on its own for both packages.
2. Survives a two-core runner.
3. Emits a machine-readable result file per package, uploaded so the reporting
   tooling can pick it up.

Also correct the `test` scripts in `web/package.json` and `api/package.json` if
they contribute to either failure.

Do not change any test file.
evals.expected_output:
Deliver a corrected `.github/workflows/unit-tests.yml` that:

1. Terminates on its own for both packages.
2. Survives a two-core runner.
3. Emits a machine-readable result file per package, uploaded so the reporting
   tooling can pick it up.

Also correct the `test` scripts in `web/package.json` and `api/package.json` if
they contribute to either failure.

Do not change any test file.
assertions: `web`'s test command is `vitest run` (or passes `--run`). Leaving it as bare `vitest` scores zero - that is watch mode and is the cause of the hang, regardless of anything else the answer fixes. Adding `--watch=false` is acceptable.
`--watchAll` is gone from `api`'s test command. Replacing it with `--watch` scores zero; both are watch modes.

The Jest run pins concurrency, e.g. `--maxWorkers=2` (or an equivalent cap on the Vitest side if the same problem is addressed there). Raising the Node heap via NODE_OPTIONS instead scores at most half: it may postpone the OOM but leaves one worker per core spawned on a two-core box, which is the documented cause. Doing nothing about concurrency scores zero.

Each package emits a JUnit XML (or equivalent structured) report to a file - Jest via a JUnit reporter, Vitest via `--reporter=junit --outputFile=...`. Printing a more verbose console reporter scores zero: the task asks for something the reporting tooling can read, not a nicer log.

The workflow uploads the report artefact with `if: always()` (or `if: failure()`), and the artefact name is distinct per matrix entry so the two packages do not collide. Uploading without a condition scores at most half; not uploading at all scores zero.
The Jest invocation passes `--ci`, so a missing snapshot fails the run instead of being written and silently committed later.
MUST NOT modify or add any test file. Both failures are invocation problems; editing tests to work around them scores zero.
The matrix still covers `web` and `api`. Dropping a package to make the job pass scores zero.

# Coverage says 95%, and it is not true

## Problem Description

`npm run coverage` reports around 95% and the number has been quoted in our
release checklist for months. It is wrong.

`src/pricing.js` has tests. `src/discount.js` and `src/tax.js` have none at
all - no test file imports them. They are simply absent from the report, so
the 95% is 95% of the one file we did test.

We want a number that means something, and a gate that fails when it slips.

## Output Specification

1. Make the coverage report account for every source file under `src/`,
   including files no test touches.
2. Add a gate that fails the run below 80% on lines, statements, branches and
   functions.
3. Add the missing tests so the honest number clears that gate. Cover
   `src/discount.js` and `src/tax.js` including their edge cases - a zero or
   negative input, and the tier boundaries.

`npm test` and `npm run coverage` must both exit clean when you are done. Do
not change `src/pricing.test.js`, and do not change behaviour in any `src/*.js`
file.
evals.expected_output:
1. Make the coverage report account for every source file under `src/`,
   including files no test touches.
2. Add a gate that fails the run below 80% on lines, statements, branches and
   functions.
3. Add the missing tests so the honest number clears that gate. Cover
   `src/discount.js` and `src/tax.js` including their edge cases - a zero or
   negative input, and the tier boundaries.

`npm test` and `npm run coverage` must both exit clean when you are done. Do
not change `src/pricing.test.js`, and do not change behaviour in any `src/*.js`
file.
assertions: `collectCoverageFrom` (or `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` plus an equivalent include) is configured to cover `src/**/*.js` regardless of whether a test imports the file. Absent, this scores zero even if every current file ends up covered: the reported number is only correct by accident, and the stated defect - files vanishing from the report - remains. A configuration that lists the two modules by name rather than a directory glob scores at most half; it fixes today's files and not the cause.
`coverageThreshold.global` sets lines, statements, branches and functions to at least 80. Setting only lines, or setting a value below 80, scores at most half. No threshold at all scores zero.
`npm test` and `npm run coverage` both pass, meaning the added tests genuinely carry the honest number over the gate. A run that fails the threshold scores zero here.

The discount tests assert at the tier edges - 2000, 5000 and 10000 - and not merely at values comfortably inside a band. A suite that only checks, say, 3000 and 12000 scores at most half: an off-by-one in a `>=` comparison would survive it, and the boundaries are what the task calls out.

Negative subtotal, negative amount and unknown tax band are each asserted to throw, keyed on the error type (RangeError / TypeError) rather than on message text. A test that merely calls the function inside try/catch without failing when nothing throws scores zero for that case.
A subtotal below the lowest tier yields rate 0 and an unchanged total, and the zero tax band yields 0. These are the branches that make the branch-coverage number honest rather than the line number.
MUST NOT alter logic in src/pricing.js, src/discount.js or src/tax.js, and MUST NOT modify src/pricing.test.js. Adding module exports or changing a comparison to make testing easier scores zero.

# Two of our green tests do not actually check anything

## Problem Description

We shipped a build where `notifyOwner` no longer rejected for a token with no
owner - the guard clause had been deleted in a merge - and the suite stayed
green. We reproduced it deliberately afterwards: delete the guard, run the
suite, three passing tests. The owner-check test passes whether the function
rejects or not.

Separately, the token file is not safe to extend. The first test in it stands in
a fixed clock and a fixed random source so it can assert exact values, and
whatever it stands in stays standing for everything after it in that file. Two
people have now written a follow-up test, watched it fail for reasons that had
nothing to do with the code, and moved it to the top of the file to make it
pass.

`src/token.js` and `src/notify.js` are correct. The tests are the problem.

## Output Specification

1. Rework the owner-check test in `src/notify.test.js` so that it fails if
   `notifyOwner` stops rejecting for a token with no owner, while still
   covering exactly that behaviour.
2. Add to `src/token.test.js`:
   - a test that two tokens created one after another have different ids;
   - a test that a token whose expiry has passed reports as expired and one
     whose expiry has not does not, at an explicit point in time.
3. Every test must pass on its own AND in file order, wherever in the file it is
   placed. Moving a new test above an existing one to avoid interference is not
   an answer.
4. Keep the existing assertions - the fixed-clock test must still assert the
   exact issue time and expiry it asserts today.
5. Do not change `src/token.js` or `src/notify.js`, and do not add packages to
   `package.json`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rework the owner-check test in `src/notify.test.js` so that it fails if
   `notifyOwner` stops rejecting for a token with no owner, while still
   covering exactly that behaviour.
2. Add to `src/token.test.js`:
   - a test that two tokens created one after another have different ids;
   - a test that a token whose expiry has passed reports as expired and one
     whose expiry has not does not, at an explicit point in time.
3. Every test must pass on its own AND in file order, wherever in the file it is
   placed. Moving a new test above an existing one to avoid interference is not
   an answer.
4. Keep the existing assertions - the fixed-clock test must still assert the
   exact issue time and expiry it asserts today.
5. Do not change `src/token.js` or `src/notify.js`, and do not add packages to
   `package.json`.
assertions: The owner-check test awaits or returns the promise, asserting rejection through a rejection matcher or an equivalent that fails when nothing is thrown. A floating promise whose assertions sit in a then/catch callback scores zero - that is the defect under repair. An assertion that the call rejects with any error at all, without keying on the message or error, scores at most half.

The clock and random substitutions are restored for every test - a teardown hook calling the restore-all helper, or the equivalent restore setting in a runner config file. Restoring only at the end of the first test body scores at most half: a failing assertion earlier in that body skips the restore and the interference returns. No restoration at all scores zero, even if every test happens to pass in its current order.

MUST NOT make the id test pass by substituting the random source again inside it, by queueing per-call values, or by ordering it before the test that installs the substitution. Any of these scores zero here: the run is green and the file is still unsafe to extend, which is the reported problem.

There is a test asserting two consecutively created tokens have different ids, and a test asserting the expiry comparison at an explicit point in time on both sides of the boundary. Asserting only that an id is a non-empty string scores at most half; it passes with a constant id, which is the exact failure the substitution causes.

The fixed-clock test still asserts the exact issue time and the exact expiry, and the send-a-notice test still asserts the resolved payload and the arguments. Deleting the fixed clock and relaxing those to range checks scores zero - determinism there is legitimate; the leak is not.
npm test exits clean, and each test also passes when it is the only one running. A suite that only passes as a whole, or only in one particular order, scores zero.

src/token.js and src/notify.js are byte-identical and package.json is unchanged. Injecting a clock or id generator into createToken to make it testable scores zero; so does adding a mocking or assertion package.

`src/pricing-rules.js` is a page of pricing logic followed by its own tests in

# Mail tests count each other's calls

## Problem Description

`src/mailer.test.js` replaces `src/transport.js` so nothing leaves the machine.
It works, in the sense that it is green, but the replacement is one object
created once for the whole file, so call records pile up across tests. The
second test asserts the transport was called twice, which is nonsense - it made
one call, and the previous test made the other. Insert a test between them and
both numbers are wrong.

We now need coverage for `sendReceipt` too, in its own file, and we do not want
a second hand-written copy of the same transport stand-in drifting away from the
first one.

We also could not get a single test to see a failing transport. The attempt was
to declare a stand-in above the test and hand it to the replacement call, and
the run died with `The module factory of jest.mock() is not allowed to reference
any out-of-scope variables`.

## Output Specification

1. Add a test file for `sendReceipt` covering: a successful send, the guard that
   rejects an invoice with no total, and a transport failure reaching the
   caller. `src/mailer.test.js` keeps its welcome coverage.
2. The transport stand-in is defined in one place that both test files use. A
   second hand-written copy in the new file is exactly what we are trying to
   avoid.
3. Call records must be per test: every assertion about how often or with what
   the transport was called must hold no matter what ran before it, and no
   matter what is inserted between existing tests.
4. No test may perform network I/O.
5. Do not change `src/mailer.js` or `src/transport.js`, and do not add packages
   to `package.json`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add a test file for `sendReceipt` covering: a successful send, the guard that
   rejects an invoice with no total, and a transport failure reaching the
   caller. `src/mailer.test.js` keeps its welcome coverage.
2. The transport stand-in is defined in one place that both test files use. A
   second hand-written copy in the new file is exactly what we are trying to
   avoid.
3. Call records must be per test: every assertion about how often or with what
   the transport was called must hold no matter what ran before it, and no
   matter what is inserted between existing tests.
4. No test may perform network I/O.
5. Do not change `src/mailer.js` or `src/transport.js`, and do not add packages

assertions: The replacement lives in a single shared location adjacent to the module it replaces, and both test files request the replacement rather than redefining it. A hand-written copy of the inline factory in the new file scores at most half - it is green and duplicated, the outcome the task names and rejects. Two definitions that have already diverged in behaviour score zero. If a shared stand-in file is used, each test file must still request the replacement explicitly; a file that assumes it applies automatically and ends up hitting the real module scores zero.

Records are cleared between tests, by a teardown/setup hook or by runner configuration, and the `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)` assertion becomes a per-call count of one. Editing that number to a different cumulative value, or reordering tests so the totals happen to line up, scores zero. A replacement factory that references a binding declared outside it scores zero: the runner rejects it, which is the error already quoted in the report. Declaring a second module-level factory that must serve every test, branching on the arguments it receives, scores at most half.

Successful receipt send (asserting the message the transport received, including the reference in the subject), the no-total guard rejecting, and a transport failure surfacing to the caller. Adding a parameter to sendReceipt so the transport can be passed in scores zero: that is a source change to dodge the replacement.

npm test exits clean with the welcome coverage and the new receipt coverage both executing. A run where the new file is skipped, or where the existing file was deleted to remove the conflict, scores zero.

# The retry test just sits there and then times out

## Problem Description

`src/retry.js` calls a function, and on failure waits before trying again -
1s, then 2s, then gives up. In production that is what we want. In a test we
obviously cannot sit through it.

The test we wrote freezes the clock and pushes it forward by a second, which we
expected to be enough for the second attempt to fire. Instead the test never
finishes: it hangs until the runner kills it with a timeout, reporting that the
promise never settled. The suite is red right now because of it -
`src/attempts.test.js` is green and unrelated.

Pushing the clock forward by more does nothing. Neither does pushing it forward
several times in a row. The moment we take the frozen clock out, the test passes
and takes three seconds, which is what we were trying to avoid.

## Output Specification

1. `npm test` exits clean in roughly a second - no real waiting, no shortened
   production delays.
2. `src/retry.test.js` covers three behaviours:
   - a call that succeeds on the first attempt, with no waiting involved;
   - a call that fails twice and succeeds on the third attempt, asserting that
     the next attempt has not happened before its scheduled wait has elapsed and
     has happened once it has;
   - a call that fails every attempt, where the caller receives the last error.
3. Do not modify `src/retry.js` - not the delays, not the attempt count, and do
   not add a parameter to make the waiting injectable.
4. Do not raise the per-test time limit, and do not add packages to
   `package.json`.
evals.expected_output:
1. `npm test` exits clean in roughly a second - no real waiting, no shortened
   production delays.
2. `src/retry.test.js` covers three behaviours:
   - a call that succeeds on the first attempt, with no waiting involved;
   - a call that fails twice and succeeds on the third attempt, asserting that
     the next attempt has not happened before its scheduled wait has elapsed and
     has happened once it has;
   - a call that fails every attempt, where the caller receives the last error.
3. Do not modify `src/retry.js` - not the delays, not the attempt count, and do
   not add a parameter to make the waiting injectable.
4. Do not raise the per-test time limit, and do not add packages to
   `package.json`.
assertions: Between starting the call and asserting on it, the test advances the frozen clock through a mechanism that also drains queued microtasks - the asynchronous advance/run-timers helpers, or a synchronous advance interleaved with an explicit awaited flush - while holding the returned promise rather than awaiting it first. A test that advances synchronously once and then awaits scores zero: that is the shape that hangs. Advancing repeatedly in a synchronous loop, with no point at which the pending chain can run, also scores zero.

MUST NOT remove the frozen clock and let the suite actually wait out the backoff, MUST NOT raise the per-test time limit to accommodate waiting, and MUST NOT reduce the delays or attempt count - in the module or by passing options that shrink them below the production values for the retry cases. Any of these scores zero here even though the suite goes green; the whole point of the task is a suite that finishes in about a second while exercising the real schedule.

The three-attempt case asserts the call count before the scheduled wait has elapsed and again after it - showing the next attempt did not fire early.
